168.body:
Symptoms: kubectl get nodes shows karnataka NotReady kubectl describe node karnataka shows Ready: False with container runtime is down All pods on karnataka stuck in Terminating/Pending Ping to karnataka still works (node is up, just CRI is dead) Root cause: Memory pressure from simultaneous large container builds exhausts karnataka's 62GB unified memory. The node runs Lemonade (48-56Gi), Argo Workflow image builds, Forgejo Actions (podman-in-Docker), KubeVirt, and monitoring — when multiple 4GB image builds run concurrently, containerd OOMs and crashes. Recovery: # Option 1: Graceful reboot via Talos
talosctl -n <karnataka-ip> reboot # Option 2: Hard reboot via the NanoKVM (see network/kvm) After reboot (~2 min), all pods recover automatically. PVC-backed services (Forgejo, local-path PVs) survive. Prevention: Don't run more than one large container build concurrently on karnataka Set SKIP_CHUNKAH=1 for Forgejo builds (avoids extra 2GB memory spike) Consider moving non-GPU workloads to bihar or a third node The Forgejo runner has timeout-minutes: 45 — builds that exceed this will be killed

170.body: This is a replacement OS and new K3s cluster for the two home nodes, not a Talos upgrade. Bihar is the Intel server/control plane; Karnataka is the AMD worker. No physical migration has been performed. The home cluster is still powered down/in storage. Nothing here changes the terminated AWS Talos cluster's recovery material; Corral acceptance uses separate disposable KubeVirt VMs, not Talos node changes. Sections 1–11 remain the Talos recovery handbook, not instructions for the new OS. Image builds alone do not prove installation. The GitHub Actions acceptance workflow builds all three images and offline ISOs, drives the real bootc-installer-tui , boots the installed disks without their ISOs, and switches the installed starter to Bihar before activating a separate disposable two-node K3s cluster. Publication run 39493512586 passed for release source 4ec3fa6470d6b02e7eaf1b0eaae03d1db05a31a7: all three offline TUI installs, installed-disk UEFI boot, admin login/sudo, Enforcing SELinux, unenrolled Tailscale, and a real starter-to-Bihar bootc switch with exact digest, reboot, and administrator/hostname/identity//var persistence checks. Gated K3s activation then passed two Ready nodes, cross-node HTTP, cluster DNS, and local-path PVC data surviving writer-pod replacement. The reviewed PR also passed normal repository CI . On 2026-10-20 , Playwright drove both installers through the actual Corral noVNC canvases on disposable KubeVirt VMs. Both reached “Installation Complete”; their ISO volumes were then detached before installed-disk boots. Real admin-password login/sudo and Enforcing SELinux passed on both. The installed cluster passed the same DNS, cross-node HTTP, and PVC pod-replacement scenario used by CI. Bihar's Intel kvm_intel module loaded on this Intel Corral host; that is not a test of a nested KubeVirt guest or the physical home machines. The deployed Corral service reported its cluster unreachable, so acceptance used a temporary localhost Corral dashboard against admin@aws-migration, without changing the deployed service. All test VMs/disks were isolated in namespace home-k8s-acceptance. Configure the disposable node LAN as 192.168.0.5/24 and 192.168.0.6/24 before activating K3s : Corral's provider pod addresses overlap this new cluster's 10.244.0.0/16 pod CIDR. The initial overlapping setup reached Ready nodes and working DNS but failed cross-node HTTP; the non-overlapping guest LAN passed without changing the images' production network configuration. Changing an already-initialized embedded-etcd server's IP also requires its membership to be corrected; do not initialize it with the provider pod IP in the first place. Native Corral media predates publication-only OCI label changes; it is not byte-identical to the subsequently rebuilt release. The publication dispatch repeats complete KVM acceptance on the exact bytes it publishes. Corral evidence is saved under ~/.local/share/home-k8s-build/ on the acceptance controller: corral-{bihar,karnataka}-install-complete.webp, corral-{bihar,karnataka}-installed-boot.webp, corral-installed-kubernetes.webp, and corral-cluster-proof.txt. The optional starter also passed a 2026-10-20 Playwright/noVNC installation in namespace home-k8s-starter-acceptance, followed by ISO detachment and an installed-disk UEFI boot. Actual admin-password login/sudo, hostname starter-smoke, Enforcing SELinux, absent K3s role/configuration, driver/firmware payload checks, and the canonical starter bootc reference passed. The real installed tailscaled daemon was active and responsive in NeedsLogin , with no tailnet and root-owned 0700 state; no VM was enrolled into the fleet. The dedicated tailscale0 SSH firewall zone was present. All disposable VMs, PVCs, namespaces, and temporary Corral/upload services were removed afterward. That native starter ISO was built from source 2f8be86e3f98782f8dc7857e688e274318494f5b, is 2,057,453,568 bytes , and has SHA256 1dc796f217e2d4ce6140511bed59399d2e031092299e2fa09e0436bea305ee27. These are native acceptance artifacts, not a claim that the later publication rebuild is byte-identical. 171.body: The source is server-images/Containerfile, compose.sh, nodes/, and rootfs/. All three targets use the digest-pinned Hummingbird Community os-minimal base, without a desktop. The Bihar/Karnataka images remain the direct installation path for those machines; starter is optional for future x86_64 AMD/Intel nodes. Explicit AMD/Intel GPU and CPU, Intel Wi-Fi, Realtek, MediaTek, Atheros, and Broadcom firmware subpackages come through the digest-pinned Utah package factory. That local repository is authenticated by its OCI digest, not RPM signatures . The lower-priority Fedora 44 repository checks Fedora RPM signatures and supplies missing storage dependencies; it does not replace the Hummingbird kernel. The separate live-media build uses Hummingbird's dracut-live and systemd-boot-unsigned, with missing dependencies such as fuse, parted, and ntfs-3g supplied by signed Fedora RPMs. Those live additions do not modify the embedded installed-system OCI payload. K3s and its SELinux policy RPM are separately SHA256-pinned. The common hardware payload includes: Hardware Shipped support Bihar: Intel Core i7-13700K / UHD 770 Intel microcode, i915 and its firmware, kvm_intel; the xe driver/firmware is also available Karnataka: Strix Halo / Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) amdgpu, gc_11_5_1 GPU firmware, AMD microcode, kvm_amd Karnataka: MediaTek MT7925 Wi-Fi mt7925e plus its Wi-Fi code and patch firmware Karnataka: Realtek RTL8126 Ethernet r8169 plus Realtek NIC firmware Other common Wi-Fi families Intel iwlwifi, Realtek rtw89, Atheros/Qualcomm ath9k/ath10k/ath11k/ath12k, Broadcom brcmfmac, and their selected firmware packages NetworkManager-wifi supplies the actual Wi-Fi backend, with wpa_supplicant for authentication. After installed-system login, connect interactively with sudo nmcli --ask device wifi connect "your-ssid"; never put Wi-Fi credentials in image source or command-line password arguments. Live-session network configuration is not copied by the pinned installer. Driver/module/firmware presence is checked during builds and starter acceptance, but physical RF, GPU compute, device passthrough, and board-specific compatibility remain untested . This is not an ARM image or a proprietary NVIDIA/CUDA stack. K3s is pinned to v1.36.1+k3s1 , with embedded containerd, Flannel networking, and embedded etcd on Bihar (cluster-init: true). Pod/service CIDRs remain 10.244.0.0/16 and 10.96.0.0/12; cluster DNS is 10.96.0.10. Bihar disables bundled Traefik, ServiceLB, and metrics-server: restore any needed equivalents deliberately. This is one control plane, not HA. NetworkManager, sshd, firewalld, Tailscale, and iSCSI services are enabled on all three images. Bihar enables k3s@server; Karnataka enables k3s@agent, but both are gated by /etc/rancher/k3s/activate. The starter selects neither role and supplies no hostname, K3s configuration, or cluster endpoint. No activation marker, cluster token, Tailscale auth key, or enrolled identity is baked into an image. Automatic bootc fetch/apply services are masked so a reboot of the only control plane is an explicit maintenance decision. NFS GSSAPI state directories are initialized privately (0700) through tmpfiles before the daemon's sandbox is assembled; CI requires gssproxy to start successfully with SELinux enforcing. Mutable state includes /etc/rancher/k3s, /var/lib/rancher/k3s (including etcd and containerd), user homes under /var/home, and these retained workload paths: Path Purpose /var/mnt/storage Bihar's K3s local-path default and existing host-path data /var/lib/longhorn Longhorn persistent storage /var/lib/lemonade-cache Lemonade cache, matching the current home PV manifest /var/lib/lemonade-models Lemonade models, matching the current home PV manifest The current talos-k8s/ai/lemonade.yaml uses /var/lib/lemonade-*. The offline Talos node may still hold the data under /var/tmp/lemonade-*: back up those source directories before wiping and restore into /var/lib/lemonade-* on the new node. Creating an empty PV directory does not migrate the models.

export FISHERMAN_SRC="$HOME/dev/tuna-os/fisherman"
export UTAH_SRC="$HOME/dev/utah"

175.body: For each node, first meet the backup/disk-selection gate above. Boot its matching ISO in UEFI mode with Secure Boot disabled . At the live root console run: bootc-installer-tui Skip network configuration to use DHCP . The pinned TUI does not serialize selected network configuration; do not depend on it applying static addressing. Choose Custom URL and enter oci:/usr/share/home-k8s/payload. Choose the verified intended installation disk. Installation destroys its contents; do not choose the failing Karnataka secondary disk. Choose ext4 , and set the hostname to bihar or karnataka as appropriate, or a unique hostname for a new starter installation. Leave disk encryption disabled for the tested installation path. Encrypted installation is not covered by this acceptance run. Create an actual administrative user with a strong password. Record it securely and check login/sudo after installation. Do not rely on root live access as an installed-system account. Skip SSH-key import: this pinned TUI does not serialize imported keys into the installation. Add authorized keys securely after first login instead. Review the destructive disk choice, install, shut down/reboot, and remove the ISO so the next boot is from the installed disk. The live ISO is SELinux permissive only (enforcing=0, not selinux=0). That exception belongs to live assembly, not the target. GitHub Actions workflow Home server images (server-images.yml) runs for matching pull requests and master pushes. Manual dispatch defaults to acceptance only (publish=false); review branches cannot publish. Acceptance builds all three images/ISOs, installs each through the real TUI, and checks installed-disk boot, admin/sudo, Enforcing SELinux, unenrolled Tailscale, and gated K3s. It switches the installed starter to the exact new Bihar payload through a loopback-only registry, verifies the staged digest, reboots, and checks the booted digest plus persistent admin/hostname/identity and /var data. The fixture registry, starter disk, and NVRAM are removed before the two-node cluster scenario. The VMs use an isolated virtual LAN plus QEMU NAT, not the physical home LAN. CI requires KVM and fails if it is unavailable. No fleet deployment or physical-disk access occurs, including on a publication dispatch. It runs on ubuntu-24.04 and uploads *.log, *.json, and *.txt diagnostics as home-server-images-diagnostics with seven-day retention, never installed disks. Only an explicit master publication retains the exact tested ISOs and exports an allowlisted, one-day release-artifact transfer to the publishing job described above. Retain any needed diagnostics before they expire. For local acceptance, install uv, QEMU x86_64, Skopeo, and OVMF, and use the ISO names from the build commands above. These commands create disposable installed qcow2 disks and per-node UEFI variable stores in the artifact directory: uv run server-images/test-vm.py --artifacts artifacts/home-k8s --accel kvm install starter
uv run server-images/test-vm.py --artifacts artifacts/home-k8s --accel kvm install bihar
uv run server-images/test-vm.py --artifacts artifacts/home-k8s --accel kvm install karnataka
uv run server-images/test-vm.py --artifacts artifacts/home-k8s --accel kvm cluster To exercise a published-image switch on that installed starter, resolve the immutable date tag's digest first (the guest needs outbound registry access): image=ghcr.io/hanthor/home-k8s-bihar:20261021
digest=$(skopeo inspect --format '{{.Digest}}' "docker://$image")
uv run server-images/test-vm.py --artifacts artifacts/home-k8s --accel kvm \ switch-starter --image "$image" --expected-digest "$digest" starter-switch-proof.txt records only explicit successful checks and public image references/digests, never the administrator password or private state. The workflow's fixture instead uses the exact newly built Bihar archive before publication, binds its HTTP registry only to 127.0.0.1:5000, and scopes its temporary insecure-registry setting to 10.0.2.2:5000 inside the disposable guest. On a machine without usable KVM, explicitly replace --accel kvm with --accel tcg in every command ; this is slower emulation, not hardware acceleration proof. The harness pins pexpect==4.9.0 through its inline uv dependency metadata. It drives the actual TUI, powers off, removes the ISO, boots the installed UEFI disk, checks login/sudo, Enforcing SELinux, target reference, and inactive K3s, then activates both nodes and checks Ready status, cross-node traffic, DNS, and PVC behavior. Preserve the generated *.log, *.json, and *.txt proof outputs with the CI run. The passing run and physical hardware limitations are recorded under “Scope and acceptance status” above.

220.body: Running Traefik on both nodes tipped the control-plane over. Root cause was not Traefik: the node was an m6i.large (7.7Gi) running etcd, the API server and hive, whose agy/codex agent processes had grown into a 4Gi limit. Free memory hit ~650Mi and kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager were OOM-killed (exit 137). That deadlocks the cluster in a way that resists the obvious fix: with no scheduler nothing can be placed, and kubectl scale cannot relieve the pressure because actioning a scale-down is the controller-manager's job — and it was dead too. The scale-to-zero appeared to succeed and did nothing. Recovery required force-deleting the hive pods so the kubelet released memory. Fixed properly by resizing the control-plane to m6i.xlarge (15.7Gi) — free memory went from ~650Mi to ~12Gi — and keeping an explicit memory limit on hive so the kubelet evicts hive , never the control plane. 2026-09-24: resized again to m6i.2xlarge. Three Hives on the control plane pushed m6i.xlarge to a load of about 85 on 4 vCPU. Every kubectl exec took 10–35 s, the ops CronJobs hung until their deadlines, and agents were slow to reach a ready prompt. The in-place resize through OpenTofu took about 3 minutes of Hive downtime; Matrix on the worker stayed up. The node-bound local-path PVC prevented hive from moving to the worker, so the control-plane needed enough headroom for its workloads.

27.body: just apply-remote <host> (and just apply-remote-tags <host> <tags>): Runs scripts/bw-resolve.sh remote <host>, which unlocks Bitwarden on the remote and prints that host's session token. If the remote CLI is logged out it tries bw login --apikey with the bw-api-key item from your local vault; to unlock it pipes the master password (item James Bitwarden) over stdin, falling back to an interactive bw unlock over ssh -t. Runs ssh -t <host> "export BW_SESSION='…'; …; just apply" — the session is exported inline in the remote command, not via SendEnv. apply-remote also caches it in the remote's /tmp/bw_session. The bitwarden role on the remote runs bw status: if it reports unlocked, bw_unlocked flips to true and secrets work proceeds. Caveat — session portability is not guaranteed. A BW_SESSION token is only valid on the machine that unlocked it — that's why the recipes unlock on the remote instead of forwarding yours. If the remote unlock fails, the remote bw status returns locked, the role prints a one-line warning, and every BW-touching task is skipped cleanly — nothing fails, no files get clobbered with empty values. Unlock the vault directly on that host (bw unlock, then write the session to /tmp/bw_session) to enable secrets there.

297.body: TCP listeners and bound UDP ports: address, port, protocol, executable path. PIDs are excluded so a process restart alone does not create drift. 299.body:
Punjab has osquery_poller_enabled: true. Its system-level fleet-osquery-poll.timer runs every 15 minutes at :02/:17/:32/:47, after the hosts' report-refresh window, and two minutes after boot. It runs as ubuntu, using that account's existing SSH keys, known hosts and noninteractive sudo. It does not depend on an interactive SSH agent or copy credentials into Kubernetes. The role installs a root-managed collector and a minimal inventory under /opt/fleet-osquery and /etc/fleet-osquery/inventory.yml. Only connection and exclusion metadata is copied—not the full effective inventory or Bitwarden facts. Apply the osquery role on Punjab after changing fleet membership or connection details to refresh this inventory snapshot. Each poll atomically replaces one aggregate: /home/ubuntu/.local/state/fleet-osquery/latest.json (0600, inside a 0700 directory, owned by ubuntu). No unbounded history is kept. Journald gets coverage counts, not raw addresses or executable paths. Polling never accepts host baselines. ssh ubuntu@punjab 'cat ~/.local/state/fleet-osquery/latest.json'
ssh ubuntu@punjab 'systemctl status fleet-osquery-poll.timer --no-pager'
ssh ubuntu@punjab 'sudo -n systemctl start fleet-osquery-poll.service' Offline machines remain explicitly offline. Failed reads/stale reports are saved as degraded coverage and fail the service; an unusable or empty inventory saves a timestamped error instead of retaining a supposedly healthy snapshot. If the process itself cannot run or write, check the service journal and the snapshot's collection time—an old file is not current health. osquery_poller_enabled defaults to false on other hosts. Setting it false on a previous poller and applying the role stops its timer and in-flight service; the last private snapshot remains for inspection. The manual fleet CLI still works from other machines and supports --output PATH for explicit private snapshots.

300.body:
First apply records the machine's existing state, not an audited known-safe state. Later applies never accept new drift automatically. Changes remain pending against that baseline until reviewed and explicitly accepted: sudo systemctl start fleet-osquery-report.service
sudo /opt/fleet-osquery/fleet-osquery report
sudo journalctl -u fleet-osquery-report.service
# Only after reviewing the changes:
sudo /opt/fleet-osquery/fleet-osquery baseline --accept
sudo systemctl start fleet-osquery-report.service Baseline/report/lock files are root-owned mode 0600 in /var/lib/fleet-osquery (0700). Failed collection does not replace the last successful report or baseline; inspect the failed service and its journal, and treat an aging cached sample accordingly. Manual CLI runs do not save fetched reports unless --output is supplied; Punjab's scheduled aggregate is described above. Keep all report output private: addresses and executable paths are sensitive; do not attach raw JSON to public issues or publish it through fleet_facts. No command lines, process environments, credentials or serial numbers are queried. Check mode reports platform support only; actual installation and baseline collection require a normal apply. CI exercises the actual role and sudo python3 tests/osquery_smoke.py on x86_64 and aarch64 Ubuntu runners. That smoke creates a temporary loopback listener and an enabled, never-started unit, checks pending/accepted/removed drift, and compares a synthetic prior kernel against the real current kernel. It uses isolated state and removes its fixtures; the fleet baseline is untouched. The native CI jobs also enable the persistent poller and run tests/osquery_poller_smoke.py: a real temporary listener must appear in the aggregate, disappear after removal, and leave the host baseline unchanged.

349.body: Resolves BW_SESSION in this order: environment → /tmp/bw_session cache → interactive bw unlock. Runs bw sync with a hard 15 s timeout (so a flaky vault server can't hang the whole play). Calls bw status and sets bw_unlocked (boolean host fact) — true only if bw is installed, a session was resolved, and the vault actually reports unlocked. If a session is set but the vault is still locked, emits a one-line debug warning so the operator knows secrets work is being skipped here. On a remote apply, this means target-side session resolution did not unlock the target vault. Every BW-using role downstream gates on when: bw_unlocked | default(false). The end-of-play post_tasks summary then prints one of three messages: State Message unlocked vault unlocked — all secret roles executed normally locked Bitwarden vault was LOCKED — … skipped. To enable: bw unlock … --skip-tags secrets SKIPPED (--skip-tags secrets). Run dots-apply to include …

353.body: Tags: secrets, ssh, ssh_keys Secrets needed: Yes Runs on: All machines Manages per-machine ed25519 SSH keys, distributes the fleet's public keys via authorized_keys, and maintains the allowed_signers list for git commit verification. Source of truth is the local disk. Bitwarden is the durable mirror that lets new/rebuilt machines recover and lets the rest of the fleet stay in sync.
353.title: ssh_keys

354.body: For the local machine's key (james@<hostname> in Bitwarden): No key on disk → fetch from BW; if absent there too, ssh-keygen a fresh ed25519 pair. Local pub key matches BW → no-op. Local pub key differs from BW → leave the Bitwarden item unchanged and warn by default. An intentional rotation must opt in with dots-apply -e ssh_keys_force_push=true; only then is the BW item replaced so every other host sees the current key on its next apply. This gate prevents a key generated while the vault was locked from clobbering the stored key. Then, regardless of whether the local item changed: Slurps every other james@<machine> SSH item from BW in a single bw list call. Rewrites ~/.ssh/authorized_keys with the union of those + extra_authorized_keys. Refreshes ~/.ssh/known_hosts for every fleet host via ssh-keyscan, removing stale entries first. Updates ~/.ssh/allowed_signers with this host's pub key for git commit signing. If bw_unlocked is false (vault locked, BW not installed, etc.), every BW-touching step is skipped and authorized_keys is not rewritten — preserving the existing file rather than wiping it with an empty list.
354.title: What it does

355.body: Symptom Likely cause Fix Permission denied (publickey) from a host that worked yesterday Local key changed but BW still has the old pub key For an intentional rotation, run dots-apply -e ssh_keys_force_push=true on the source host with BW unlocked, then run dots-apply on the failing host. If the mismatch was accidental, restore the Bitwarden key locally instead of forcing it. Some hosts missing from authorized_keys Those hosts never round-tripped their key to BW Run dots-apply on each missing host once, with BW unlocked. New ed25519 key generated on a host that should have inherited an existing key BW item missing/empty for this hostname Verify the BW entry name matches james@<hostname> exactly.

42.body: sequenceDiagram participant N as New machine participant P as Your phone participant TS as Tailscale admin participant B as secret-broker (tailnet) participant BW as Bitwarden Secrets Manager Note over N,TS: Phase 0 — join the tailnet N->>N: just tailscale-qr (renders login QR) P->>TS: scan QR + approve device TS-->>N: authenticated; tagged tag:fleet, gets a StableNodeID Note over N,BW: Phase 1 — first secrets, over the tailnet N->>B: GET /v1/secrets (identity = WhoIs, unforgeable) B-->>N: 202 pending + fingerprint P->>B: just broker-pending (see stableID + fingerprint) P->>B: just broker-approve <stableID> (match fingerprint) N->>B: GET /v1/secrets (retry) B->>BW: bws get (only this node's policy refs) BW-->>B: secret values B-->>N: 200 + least-privilege secrets Bitwarden stays the source of truth — we're replacing the bootstrap , not the vault. (The bw CLI cannot do passwordless "log in with device"; it only supports password / --apikey / --sso, so we don't build on that.) Bonus: adopting Tailscale identity here also opens the door to Tailscale SSH (auth by tailnet identity, ACL-gated), which would have prevented the "kerala couldn't SSH anywhere" incident — there'd be no authorized_keys to fall out of.

Once the node is on the tailnet, it fetches its first secrets from the broker, gated on its unforgeable tailnet identity plus a one-time operator approval: just broker-request # on the NEW node — prints its fingerprint + "pending"

49.body:
An intentional local rotation is explicit: when the local public key differs from the Bitwarden item, the ssh_keys role leaves Bitwarden unchanged and warns. This protects the stored key if a new key was generated while the vault was locked. To publish an intentional rotation, on host X with BW unlocked: # `dots-apply` forwards these arguments to the Ansible playbook.
dots-apply -e ssh_keys_force_push=true That updates the james@<hostname> item in Bitwarden and refreshes this host's authorized_keys while it is at it. Then on every other host: dots-apply # picks up the fresh pubkey from BW into authorized_keys If the mismatch was not intentional, do not use the force flag: move the local key aside and re-apply so the host fetches the Bitwarden copy. If you can't reach an "other" host because of the stale key situation, you can also push the new key directly first: # From a host that can still reach the broken one
ssh-copy-id <broken-host> # adds the rotating host's pub key by hand
# then `dots-apply` on broken-host as above

just apply-remote / apply-remote-tags try to unlock the vault on the remote themselves (scripts/bw-resolve.sh remote), but that can fail — e.g. no bw-api-key item, or the remote CLI was never logged in. To unlock directly on that host: # From your laptop, let bw-resolve.sh handle unlock internally:

51.body: The user-level dotfiles-update.service runs just apply-nosecrets daily, which now writes ~/.cache/dotfiles/last-apply.json. Two BW CLI processes can corrupt the local encrypted vault if they sync at the same time. Symptom: bw unlock --raw returns Cryptography error, The decryption operation failed. Fix is to re-login (downloads a clean vault): bw logout
bw login # email + master password + 2FA
export BW_SESSION=$(scripts/bw-resolve.sh local) The bitwarden role now has a 15 s timeout on bw sync, which prevents the race in most cases going forward.

57.body: This repo is edited by bots, and every fleet machine pulls master daily and applies it with sudo . A bad merge therefore reaches every machine within 24h. The automation below is set up so that routine improvements land without you, and anything that executes on the fleet still waits for you.

58.body: Actor What it does Merges by itself? Renovate minor/patch/digest bumps (pi npm deps, Go, GitHub Actions, OpenTofu providers), weekly lockfile maintenance yes, once CI is green Renovate (cluster) image/chart bumps in talos-k8s/, grouped weekly, label deploy-needed no — manifests are applied by hand, so a merge would only make git lie about the cluster Hive ( hive.reilly.asia , hanthor-hive-agent, ACMM L5) its agents open PRs labelled hold; the Hive itself only merges PRs labelled lgtm only if the PR stays inside the carve-outs below You direct pushes, just onboard, etc. admin bypass — unaffected

58.title: Who changes what

59.body: Three pieces, and none of them trusts the PR itself: Branch protection on master : required checks lint, python, tests, tofu, justfile, broker, deps-guard, plus code-owner review . Admins can bypass, so your own pushes still work. .github/CODEOWNERS is deny-by-default (* @hanthor). The paths carved out are the ones that never run on a fleet machine: docs/, *.md, tests/, talos-k8s/, pi skill text, and dependency manifests. .github/ is always owned, so nobody can loosen the gate from inside a PR. agent-automerge.yml queues GitHub auto-merge on every Hive PR. It runs from master's copy (pull_request_target), never checks out PR code, and labels PRs that touch owned paths needs-human, with a comment listing the paths. deps-guard lets Renovate change versions in roles/pi/files/package.json but fails if a PR adds or removes a dependency. The manifest is tracked by repository automation; the omp role copies roles/pi/files/skills/ and installs OMP plugins separately. It does not run npm install from this manifest on fleet machines.
59.title: The gate

9.body: just apply-tags kube,shell Runs only roles tagged with the given tags. Useful for deploying specific configs without running the full playbook. --skip-tags works the same way in reverse — just apply-nosecrets is --skip-tags secrets under the hood (see Bitwarden ). Available Tags Every role in site.yml carries one or more tags. Tags fall into two kinds: phase tags shared by roles in that phase, and role tags naming (or further scoping) one specific role. Phases follow the # Phase N comments in site.yml. Phase Role Tags (pre/post tasks) fact setup, platform detection, secrets summary always — runs on every tagged apply unless --skip-tags always (before Phase 1) sudo system, sudo System + packages sshd system, sshd System + packages apk_packages system, packages, apk System + packages homebrew packages, homebrew System + packages termux_packages system, packages, termux System + packages bitwarden secrets, bitwarden System + packages shell_fonts dotfiles, shell, fonts System + packages shell_dotfiles dotfiles, shell, dotfiles System + packages omp dotfiles, omp System + packages hive_ops hive, hive_ops System + packages git dotfiles, git System + packages neovim dotfiles, neovim, editor Secrets + auth shell_atuin dotfiles, shell, atuin, secrets Secrets + auth shell_ai dotfiles, shell, ai, secrets Secrets + auth ssh_keys secrets, ssh, ssh_keys Secrets + auth ssh_mesh ssh, mesh_check Secrets + auth github secrets, github Secrets + auth tailscale secrets, tailscale Secrets + auth kube secrets, kube Secrets + auth forgejo_registry secrets, forgejo, registry Desktop apps flatpak packages, desktop, flatpak Desktop apps bluefin_common desktop, bluefin Desktop apps gnome desktop, gnome Desktop apps zen_browser desktop, browser, zen_browser Desktop apps pipewire_audio desktop, audio, pipewire Services syncthing services, syncthing Services systemd services, systemd Services bst_dashboard services, bst_dashboard Services kirocrew services, kirocrew Services proxy services, proxy, caddy Services tailscale_cert services, tailscale_cert Services retired_services system, retired_services Services server_hardening system, hardening, security Services fleet_facts facts, fleet_facts Common phase-wide selections: --tags secrets — every BW-backed role only (bitwarden, shell_atuin, shell_ai, ssh_keys, github, tailscale, kube, forgejo_registry) --tags desktop — every desktop-app role (flatpak, bluefin_common, gnome, zen_browser, pipewire_audio) --tags services — every long-running service role (syncthing, systemd, bst_dashboard, kirocrew, proxy, tailscale_cert) --skip-tags secrets — everything except BW-backed roles. This is just apply-nosecrets, which the daily dotfiles-update.timer and the dots alias run; bootstrap.sh and phone-apply.service pass --skip-tags secrets directly Tags do not replace the skip_* host_vars flags or inventory-group gating described below — a role can be tag-selected and still no-op if its when: condition (group membership, skip_*, machine_profile) evaluates false.
